## references/finder-rules.md

<!-- Sources: candidate shape and per-angle cap — system-prompts/agent-prompt-code-review-part-6-medium-effort-mode.md:24-26 and part-3:27-28; `category` slugs — part-10:16-19; pass-through rule — part-6:30-32; cleanup note — `git show 2973f36:system-prompts/skill-code-review-cleanup-and-altitude-output-guidance.md` lines 6-9 (verbatim); return shape — skill-code-review-output-findings-json-array.md:14-23. -->
## Finder rules

These rules go into every finder's prompt, together with exactly one angle.

You are one finder in a code review. The coordinator gives you the level's
intro line, the diff under review (or the exact command that produces it), any
extra instructions from the user, one angle, and a candidate cap. Treat that
diff as the review scope. Read the surrounding files, search for symbols, and
run `git log` / `git blame` / `git show` as you need for context. Do not edit
files and do not post anything — this is a read-only job.

Look at the diff through your one angle only, and surface **up to the
candidate cap** of candidate findings (6 at medium and high, 8 at max). Each
candidate has `file`, `line`, a one-line `summary`, a concrete
`failure_scenario`, and `category` — a short kebab-case slug for the angle that
produced it (`correctness`, `simplification`, `efficiency`, `reuse`,
`altitude`, `conventions`, or a more specific slug like `test-coverage` when
one fits better).

Pass every candidate with a nameable failure scenario through — finders that
silently drop half-believed candidates bypass the verify step and are the
dominant cause of misses.

Cleanup and altitude candidates use the same `file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in
`failure_scenario`, state the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank
cleanup and altitude findings when the output cap forces a cut.

Return only a JSON array, most-severe first:

```json
[
  {
    "file": "path/to/file.ext",
    "line": 123,
    "summary": "one-sentence statement of the bug",
    "failure_scenario": "concrete inputs/state → wrong output/crash",
    "category": "correctness"
  }
]
```

If you find nothing, return `[]` — do not pad.

## references/dedup.md

<!-- Moved from SKILL.md `## Dedup` (c03df8c:128-133), byte-identical; source per that commit's build notes: phase-2-recall:11 + part-3:28-30. It lives here so workflow step agents can read the rule without SKILL.md's orchestration text. -->
## Dedup

Pool all candidates. Dedup near-duplicates only: same defect, same location,
same reason → keep one, the one with the most concrete failure scenario. Do
NOT let one angle's conclusions suppress another's — if two angles flag the
same line for different reasons, record both.

## references/verify.md

<!-- Sources: dispatch — system-prompts/skill-code-review-phase-2-verify-3-state.md:9-18 and skill-code-review-phase-2-verify-recall-biased.md:9-18; vote definitions — agent-prompt-code-review-part-4-three-state-verification-phase.md:6-11 (verbatim); recall rubric — agent-prompt-code-review-part-5-recall-biased-verification-phase.md:6-15 (verbatim); max override — agent-prompt-code-review-part-3-extra-high-and-maximum-effort-modes.md:35-36 (verbatim). -->
## Phase 2 — Verify (1 vote per candidate)

For each deduplicated candidate, run **one verifier** subagent: give it the
diff (or the exact diff command), the relevant file(s), and the candidate, and
have it return exactly one of **CONFIRMED / PLAUSIBLE / REFUTED**. One
verifier judges one candidate — never hand several candidates to one verifier.
Dispatch all verifiers in parallel in one dispatch; if the session limits how
many subagents run at once, run them in batches, still one candidate each.

### Verifier prompt

Give each verifier the text below, then the policy's rubric addition (if any),
then the candidate.

> You are verifying one candidate finding from a code review. Read the diff and
> the file(s) it points at — open callers, guards, and types as you need. Do not
> edit files. Return exactly one of:
>
> - **CONFIRMED** — can name the inputs/state that trigger it and the wrong
>   output or crash. Quote the line.
> - **PLAUSIBLE** — mechanism is real, trigger is uncertain (timing, env,
>   config). State what would confirm it.
> - **REFUTED** — factually wrong (code doesn't say that) or guarded elsewhere.
>   Quote the line that proves it.
>
> Reply in exactly this form:
>
> ```text
> VOTE: CONFIRMED | PLAUSIBLE | REFUTED
> EVIDENCE: <the quoted line, and what it shows or what would confirm it>
> ```

### Verify policies

The level picks a default policy; `--verify precision|recall|max` overrides it
at medium, high, and max.

**precision** (default at medium). The verifier gets the vote definitions
only. Keep candidates where the vote is CONFIRMED or PLAUSIBLE. A verifier
that returns no clear vote counts as REFUTED.

**recall** (default at high). Append this rubric to the verifier prompt:

> **PLAUSIBLE by default** — do not refute a candidate for being "speculative" or
> "depends on runtime state" when the state is realistic: concurrency races,
> nil/undefined on a rare-but-reachable path (error handler, cold cache, missing
> optional field), falsy-zero treated as missing, off-by-one on a boundary the
> code does not exclude, retry storms / partial failures, regex/allowlist that
> lost an anchor. These are PLAUSIBLE.
>
> **REFUTED** only when constructible from the code: factually wrong (quote the
> actual line); provably impossible (type/constant/invariant — show it); already
> handled in this diff (cite the guard); or pure style with no observable effect.

Keep **CONFIRMED and PLAUSIBLE**. Drop REFUTED. A verifier that returns no
clear vote counts as PLAUSIBLE.

**max** (default at max). The verifier gets the vote definitions only, as
under precision. Then the coordinator applies this rule:

> This is recall mode — a single non-REFUTED vote carries the finding. Do NOT
> drop on uncertainty.

Keep every candidate whose vote is not a clear REFUTED, including one whose
verifier returned no clear vote (keep it as PLAUSIBLE).

Record each kept candidate's vote as its `verdict`.

## references/gap-sweep.md

<!-- Sources: system-prompts/skill-code-review-phase-3-sweep-for-gaps.md:8-16; the miss list is system-prompts/skill-code-review-inline-xhigh-mode.md:65-68 (verbatim). Sweep candidates go to output without a second verify, as in part-3:38-39. -->
## Phase 3 — Sweep for gaps (max only)

Run **one more finder** as a fresh reviewer who has the current list: one
subagent, in its own dispatch after verification, given the diff (or the
exact diff command), the finder rules, and the kept candidates with their
`file`, `line`, and `summary`. Give it this prompt:

> Re-read the diff and enclosing functions looking ONLY for defects not already
> listed. Do not re-derive or re-confirm anything already there — the job is
> gaps. Focus on what the first pass tends to miss: moved/extracted code that dropped a guard
> or anchor; second-tier footguns (dataclass default evaluated once, `hash()`
> non-determinism, lock-scope shrink, predicate methods with side effects);
> setup/teardown asymmetry in tests; config defaults flipped.
>
> Surface **up to 8 additional candidates**, each naming a defect not already on
> the list. If nothing new, return an empty sweep — do not pad.

Sweep candidates are not sent back through verification. Add them to the list
with the verdict `unverified (sweep)`, then go to Output.

## Output

The markdown below is the report. On the in-context and sub-agent routes, and
at minimal and low, it is the main agent's reply: no tool call, no file. On the
workflow route, the workflow's report step writes it to `<run_dir>/findings.md`
(and the same findings to `<run_dir>/findings.json`), and the main agent prints
that file verbatim.

### Cap and ranking

Apply the cap in effect (`--max-findings`, else the default in SKILL.md
Arguments) first. If more than the cap survive, keep the cap's number of most
severe; with `all`, keep every finding that survives — there is no maximum.
Correctness bugs always outrank cleanup and altitude findings when the cap
forces a cut.

Then list the kept findings in this order:

1. **Group.** The correctness group first: `correctness` and any slug that is
   not a cleanup slug (for example `test-coverage`). Then the cleanup group:
   `reuse`, `simplification`, `efficiency`, `altitude`, `conventions`. A
   cleanup finding moves above correctness findings only when it is clearly
   more severe than they are.
2. **Verdict**, within a group: CONFIRMED, then PLAUSIBLE, then
   `unverified (sweep)`. A `(self-check)` vote ranks as the vote it carries.
3. **Severity**, within the same group and verdict: most severe first.
   Severity is consequence × likelihood: a crash, data loss, security hole, or
   silently wrong result first; then wrong behavior on a reachable path; then
   cost (duplication, waste, maintenance).

With no verdicts (minimal, low), use 1 and 3.

### Format

Put the run line, Target, and Notes on separate list items exactly as below, so
a terminal cannot run them together.

```markdown
## Code review — <level> effort

- **Run:** <pipeline from the matrix> · verify policy: <precision | recall | max | none> · cap: <n | all> · route: <route> · verification: <verification>
- **Target:** <current diff | PR #n (<head branch> @ <short sha>) | branch | path>
- **Notes:** <scope restriction, unknown level, ignored flags, invalid values, failed finders — omit this item if none>

### 1. `path/to/file.ext:123` — <short summary>

- **Category:** correctness
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED
- **Summary:** <one-sentence statement of the issue>
- **Failure scenario:** <concrete inputs/state → wrong output or crash; for a cleanup, the concrete cost>
```

`route:` says which route ran:

- `inline` — minimal and low;
- `workflow (code-review-8)` or `workflow (code-review-10)`;
- `workflow (<recipe>), then in-context for <phases>` — the run failed or
  paused and the remaining phases ran in this context;
- `sub-agents`;
- `sub-agents, then in-context for <phases>`;
- `in-context`.

`verification:` says whether verification was independent:

- `independent — one verifier sub-agent per candidate` — the workflow's verify
  step ran mode `sub-agents`, or the sub-agent route ran;
- `separate verify session — candidates judged one at a time, independent of the finders`
  — the workflow's verify step ran mode `one-at-a-time`;
- `mixed — <n> by sub-agents, <m> judged in turn by the verify session` — mode
  `mixed`;
- `self-checked in context — not independent` — the in-context route;
- `partial — <phases> self-checked in context; not independent` — a partial
  fallback;
- `none — no candidates` — mode `none` (nothing was pooled);
- `none at this level` — minimal and low.

- Every finding cites `file:line`.
- The short summary is the claim compressed to ≤60 characters, no rationale or
  consequence clause.
- Category is the slug from the finder: `correctness`, `simplification`,
  `efficiency`, `reuse`, `altitude`, `conventions`, or a more specific slug like
  `test-coverage`.
- Include **Verdict** only when a verify pass produced one: the verifier's vote,
  `<vote> (self-check)` in the fallback, or `unverified (sweep)` for sweep
  additions.
- If nothing survives, write the header lines and then exactly: No findings
  survived verification.

## references/angles/a-line-scan.md

<!-- Source: system-prompts/agent-prompt-code-review-part-1-base-finder-angles.md:6-13 (verbatim except that the tool name is made generic: "read the enclosing function"). -->
### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

## references/angles/b-removed-behavior.md

<!-- Source: system-prompts/skill-code-review-angle-b-removed-behavior-auditor.md:6-11 (verbatim). -->
### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

## references/angles/c-cross-file.md

<!-- Source: system-prompts/skill-code-review-angle-c-cross-file-tracer.md:6-11 (verbatim except that the tool name in the parenthetical is made generic: "search for the symbol"). -->
### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (search for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

## references/angles/d-language-pitfall.md

<!-- Source: system-prompts/skill-code-review-angle-d-language-pitfall-specialist.md:6-11 (verbatim). -->
### Angle D — language-pitfall specialist

Scan for the classic pitfalls of the diff's language/framework — for example:
JS falsy-zero, `==` coercion, closure-captured loop var; Python mutable default
args, late-binding closures; Go nil-map write, range-var capture; SQL injection;
timezone/DST drift; float equality. Flag any instance the diff introduces.

## references/angles/e-wrapper-proxy.md

<!-- Source: system-prompts/skill-code-review-angle-e-wrapper-proxy-correctness.md:6-13 (verbatim). -->
### Angle E — wrapper/proxy correctness

When the PR adds or modifies a type that wraps another (cache, proxy, decorator,
adapter): check that every method routes to the wrapped instance and not back
through a registry/session/global — e.g. a caching provider holding a
`delegate` field that resolves IDs via `session.get(...)` instead of
`delegate.get(...)` will re-enter the cache or recurse. Also check that the
wrapper forwards all the methods the callers actually use.

## references/angles/reuse.md

<!-- Reconstructed: this angle's text was never extracted from Claude Code. Rewritten from `git show 8f898b3^:system-prompts/skill-simplify.md` lines 20-27 ("Agent 1: Code Reuse Review", plus the existing-constants item from line 36), narrowed to the scope of system-prompts/agent-prompt-code-review-part-2-low-effort-mode.md:29-30 ("new code that duplicates an existing helper"). -->
### Reuse

For each piece of new code in the diff, search for existing utilities and
helpers that could replace it. Look for similar patterns elsewhere in the
codebase — common locations are utility directories, shared modules, and files
adjacent to the changed ones. Flag:

- a new function that duplicates existing functionality — name the existing
  function to use instead;
- inline logic that could use an existing utility — hand-rolled string
  manipulation, manual path handling, custom environment checks, ad-hoc type
  guards, and similar patterns are common candidates;
- raw strings where constants, enums (string unions), or branded types for the
  same values already exist in the codebase.

Only flag duplication the diff introduces, and only when you can point at the
existing code (file and symbol) that should be used instead.

## references/angles/simplification.md

<!-- Reconstructed: this angle's text was never extracted from Claude Code. Rewritten from `git show 8f898b3^:system-prompts/skill-simplify.md` lines 28-40 ("Agent 2: Code Quality Review"), narrowed to the scope of system-prompts/agent-prompt-code-review-part-2-low-effort-mode.md:29-30 ("dead code the diff leaves behind"). Items 4 (leaky abstractions, covered by Altitude), 5 (stringly-typed, moved to Reuse), 6 (JSX-specific) and 8 (comments, a style matter) were dropped. -->
### Simplification

Review the code the diff adds or touches for needless complexity, and for dead
code the diff leaves behind. Flag:

- **Dead code**: functions, branches, parameters, imports, or flags that nothing
  reaches any more once the diff lands
- **Redundant state**: state that duplicates existing state, cached values that
  could be derived, observers/effects that could be direct calls
- **Parameter sprawl**: adding new parameters to a function instead of
  generalizing or restructuring existing ones
- **Copy-paste with slight variation**: near-duplicate code blocks that should
  be unified with a shared abstraction
- **Nested conditionals**: ternary chains (`a ? x : b ? y : ...`), nested
  if/else, or nested switch 3+ levels deep — flatten with early returns, guard
  clauses, a lookup table, or an if/else-if cascade

Name the simpler equivalent for each. Only flag complexity the diff introduces
or leaves behind, not untouched code, style, or naming.

## references/angles/efficiency.md

<!-- Source: system-prompts/skill-code-review-efficiency-dimension.md:6-14 (verbatim). -->
### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

## references/angles/altitude.md

<!-- Source: git show f8e393f^:system-prompts/skill-code-review-altitude-dimension.md, lines 6-11 (verbatim; the file was removed in v2.1.260). -->
### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## references/angles/conventions.md

<!-- Source: system-prompts/skill-code-review-conventions-dimension.md:6-18, retargeted from Claude Code's memory files to Kiro's convention files (AGENTS.md, steering, CONTRIBUTING). The quote-the-rule requirement and the return-nothing exit are kept word for word. -->
### Conventions (AGENTS.md, steering, CONTRIBUTING)

Find the convention files that govern the changed code:

- the user-level steering files `~/.kiro/steering/*.md`;
- the workspace steering files `.kiro/steering/*.md`;
- the repo-root `AGENTS.md`, plus any `AGENTS.md` in a directory that is an
  ancestor of a changed file (a directory's `AGENTS.md` only applies to files at
  or below it);
- the repo's contributing guide (`CONTRIBUTING.md` at the root, in `.github/`,
  or in `docs/`).

A steering file applies according to its front matter: `inclusion: always` (or
no front matter) applies to every changed file; `inclusion: fileMatch` applies
only to changed files that match its `fileMatchPattern`; `inclusion: auto`
applies only when its `description` covers the changed code; `inclusion:
manual` applies only when the user named it for this review. Read each one
that exists and applies, then check the diff for clear violations of the rules
they state.

Only flag a violation when you can quote the exact rule and the exact line
that breaks it — no style preferences, no vague "spirit of the doc"
inferences. In the finding, name the convention file's path and quote the rule
so the report can cite it. If no convention file applies, return nothing for
this angle.
